name: FTP Backdoor Exploit
short_description: Exploit the famous vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor for instant root access.
description: In 2011, an attacker inserted a backdoor into vsftpd 2.3.4's source code. When a username contains ':)' (smiley face), it opens a shell on port 6200. This is CVE-2011-2523 and one of the easiest exploits to learn with Metasploit.
handler_message:
We've identified an FTP server at 172.20.0.15 that Cerberus forgot to decommission. Old infrastructure, legacy backups, project archives they thought no one would find.

The server runs vsftpd 2.3.4 - a version with a notorious backdoor. Someone compromised the source code years ago. A smiley face in the username opens a shell.

Cerberus never patched it. Their arrogance will be their undoing.

Get inside. See what they left behind.
episode_intro:
It started three weeks ago. A packet capture that wasn't meant for you. A scheduling conflict on a Tor relay. Someone's encrypted traffic, briefly visible.

You shouldn't have looked. But you did.

The word NIGHTFALL appeared seventeen times. Alongside it: infrastructure targets, deployment schedules, and the name of a defense contractor you'd never heard of.

Cerberus Systems.

Since then, your apartment was searched. Your accounts were probed. A car has been parked outside your building for six days.

You're in too deep to stop now. The only way out is through.
episode_outro:
The archived files paint a picture. Project schedules. Internal IP addresses. Codenames you don't recognize yet.

But one name appears repeatedly: David Chen, Senior Systems Administrator.

His employee ID is tagged on dozens of files. Recent access logs show he was downloading documents aggressively - far more than his job required.

The most recent entry is from three weeks ago. Then nothing.

A quick search confirms your suspicion. David Chen hasn't been seen since. Police say he 'left voluntarily.' His family says otherwise.

He knew something. Maybe he found what you're looking for.

Buried in the access logs, you find an IP address associated with his last login: 172.20.0.17. His office workstation. Still online.

That's your next target.

interstitial.title: Episode 1: THE FORGOTTEN DOOR
interstitial.content:
Three weeks ago, you intercepted traffic that wasn't meant for you. Encrypted communications referencing something called NIGHTFALL.

You've been piecing it together ever since. And someone has noticed.

Your apartment was searched. A car has been parked outside for days. You're running out of time.

An anonymous contact has started sending you intel. Targets. Credentials. Guidance. You don't know who they are or why they're helping.

But their first target is clear: an old FTP server that Cerberus Systems forgot to decommission.

Time to see what they left behind.

steps.title: Verify the target is running
steps.narrative: Before any engagement, verify your target. Nmap's -sV flag performs service version detection - essential for identifying exploitable software. For this server, we're looking for vsftpd 2.3.4 specifically. That version contains a backdoor inserted by an unknown attacker in 2011. Cerberus never updated it.
steps.expected: You should see: 21/tcp open ftp vsftpd 2.3.4

steps.title: Start Metasploit
steps.narrative: Metasploit is the industry-standard exploitation framework. The -q flag suppresses the banner for faster startup. Inside, you have access to thousands of exploits, payloads, and auxiliary modules. For a backdoor this well-documented, the exploit is already written.

steps.title: Search for the exploit
steps.narrative: Metasploit's search function queries its module database. The vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor is famous enough to have its own dedicated exploit. When a username containing ':)' is sent, the server opens a shell on port 6200. No authentication required.
steps.expected: You'll see exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor in the results

steps.title: Load the exploit module
steps.narrative: Loading a module changes your context. The prompt updates to show you're working with this specific exploit. Every module has options - parameters you configure before execution. This one is simple: just point it at the target.

steps.title: View module options
steps.narrative: Always review options before running an exploit. RHOSTS (Remote Hosts) is the target IP. Some exploits need credentials, ports, or payload configurations. This backdoor is elegant in its simplicity - just an IP address.
steps.expected: You'll see RHOSTS is required and currently empty

steps.title: Set the target
steps.narrative: RHOSTS accepts single IPs, ranges, or CIDR notation. Today it's one server - the forgotten FTP archive that Cerberus left exposed. Their infrastructure sprawls across networks they've lost track of. That's the gap you're walking through.

steps.title: Execute the exploit
steps.narrative: Execution. Metasploit sends a malformed username containing the trigger sequence. The backdoor activates. A shell opens on port 6200. The connection is established. You're inside Cerberus infrastructure now.

steps.title: Verify root access
steps.narrative: Raw reverse shells don't show prompts - the cursor just blinks. Don't let that fool you into thinking nothing happened. Type 'whoami' and press Enter. The backdoor runs as root. Full system access from a smiley face.

steps.title: Upgrade to a real prompt
steps.narrative: Raw shells are functional but uncomfortable - no prompt, no tab completion, Ctrl+C kills your session. Spawning an interactive bash gives you a proper terminal. Small improvement that makes exploration much easier.

steps.title: Confirm full access
steps.narrative: Two verification commands chained together. 'id' confirms you're uid 0 (root). /etc/shadow contains password hashes - only readable by root. If you can see this file, you have complete control. The system is yours.

steps.title: Explore the network
steps.narrative: The hosts file often reveals internal network structure. Docker environments add container hostnames here. Each entry is a potential pivot point - another system in the Cerberus infrastructure. Another piece of NIGHTFALL.
steps.expected: List of internal hostnames and IPs

steps.title: One-command pwn
steps.narrative: Now that you understand the attack chain, automation is appropriate. Exit your shell (type 'exit' twice) and run 'pwn vsftpd' from Kali. Same result, faster execution. But always understand what's happening under the hood before you automate.

success_criteria: You have a root shell on the Cerberus archive server. You can explore legacy files and discover what they tried to hide.
